searched: 2026-10-13. PubMed via NCBI E-utilities (esearch, esummary, efetch rettype=abstract). Every new paper's abstract was retrieved and read from its PubMed record; PMID and DOI come from that record. Papers marked 'source: reused' were verified on 2026-10-12 for corrections-evidence.json and their evidence text here is consistent with that file.
scope_note: Links between running findings and physical limitations are almost all cross-sectional or acute. 'none' means no tested link was found, or the link was tested and not supported (see note). Strength programmes improve strength and pain but have generally not been shown to change running kinematics; running-specific cues (step rate, mirror/real-time feedback, step width, trunk posture) are the interventions shown to change the running pattern. Movement analysis supports clinical judgment; it is not a diagnosis.

findings: small tibial progression (low tibial inclination through stance)

limitations.name: Limited ankle dorsiflexion range (calf/soleus stiffness or talocrural restriction)

evidence.citation: Joachim MR, Kliethermes SA, Heiderscheit BC 2024. Preinjury Knee and Ankle Mechanics during Running Are Reduced among Collegiate Runners Who Develop Achilles Tendinopathy. Med Sci Sports Exerc 56(1):128-133
evidence.result: Runners who later developed Achilles tendinopathy had less peak ankle dorsiflexion during running before injury (26.0 vs 28.7 deg) and less peak knee flexion (43.2 vs 45.9 deg).

evidence.citation: Becker J, James S, Wayner R, Osternig L, Chou LS 2017. Biomechanical Factors Associated With Achilles Tendinopathy and Medial Tibial Stress Syndrome in Runners. Am J Sports Med 45(11):2614-2621
evidence.result: Runners with Achilles tendinopathy or MTSS had less static dorsiflexion ROM (6.1 vs 11.2 deg) and longer rearfoot eversion duration (86% vs 59% of stance) than controls.

evidence.citation: Rabin A, Kozol Z, Finestone AS 2014. Limited ankle dorsiflexion increases the risk for mid-portion Achilles tendinopathy in infantry recruits: a prospective cohort study. J Foot Ankle Res 7(1):48
evidence.result: Recruits who developed mid-portion Achilles tendinopathy had less non-weight-bearing knee-bent DF ROM (21.1 vs 27.4 deg); only 5 cases.

evidence.citation: Hamstra-Wright KL, Bliven KC, Bay C 2015. Risk factors for medial tibial stress syndrome in physically active individuals such as runners and military personnel: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Br J Sports Med 49(6):362-9
evidence.result: Dorsiflexion ROM was clearly NOT a risk factor for MTSS; ankle plantarflexion ROM, BMI, navicular drop and hip ER ROM were.

limitations.note: No retrieved study directly tested whether a low knee-to-wall (WBLT) score produces reduced dorsiflexion or tibial progression during RUNNING. The running-DF link is inferred; static DF ROM relates to some injuries (Achilles) but not MTSS.

limitations.name: Low calf (soleus/gastrocnemius) strength-endurance
limitations.note: No tested link found between calf capacity and midstance dorsiflexion or tibial progression in running (none (clinical reasoning)).

compensations.text: Knee valgus / hip adduction on single-leg tasks (lateral step-down, squat) with low DF

evidence.citation: Rabin A, Portnoy S, Kozol Z 2016. The Association of Ankle Dorsiflexion Range of Motion With Hip and Knee Kinematics During the Lateral Step-down Test. J Orthop Sports Phys Ther 46(11):1002-1009
evidence.result: Low weight-bearing and non-weight-bearing DF subgroups showed greater peak hip adduction and knee external rotation during lateral step-down; low WB DF also had less peak knee flexion.

evidence.citation: Rabin A, Kozol Z 2010. Measures of range of motion and strength among healthy women with differing quality of lower extremity movement during the lateral step-down test. J Orthop Sports Phys Ther 40(12):792-800
evidence.result: Women with moderate (vs good) step-down movement quality had less knee-bent and weight-bearing ankle DF ROM; hip strength did not differ (as reported in abstract).

evidence.citation: Macrum E, Bell DR, Boling M, Lewek M, Padua D 2012. Effect of limiting ankle-dorsiflexion range of motion on lower extremity kinematics and muscle-activation patterns during a squat. J Sport Rehabil 21(2):144-50
evidence.result: Simulated DF restriction (12 deg forefoot wedge) in a double-leg squat increased knee valgus and medial knee displacement, decreased peak knee flexion and quadriceps activity.

evidence.citation: Mendonca ILA, Filho FMDN, Badicu G, et al. 2026. Analysis of Ankle Mobility and Dynamic Valgus Knee in Runners With and Without Patellofemoral Pain Syndrome. Health Sci Rep 9(6):e72051
evidence.result: Female runners with vs without PFP: no difference in WBLT (about 3.8-4.4 cm) or 2D knee valgus on step-down.

compensations.note: Shown in step-down/squat tasks, not in running.

compensations.text: Reduced knee flexion (stiffer stance knee)

evidence.citation: Rabin A, Portnoy S, Kozol Z 2016. The Association of Ankle Dorsiflexion Range of Motion With Hip and Knee Kinematics During the Lateral Step-down Test. J Orthop Sports Phys Ther 46(11):1002-1009
evidence.result: Low weight-bearing DF subgroup had decreased peak knee flexion during step-down.

evidence.citation: Joachim MR, Kliethermes SA, Heiderscheit BC 2024. Preinjury Knee and Ankle Mechanics during Running Are Reduced among Collegiate Runners Who Develop Achilles Tendinopathy. Med Sci Sports Exerc 56(1):128-133
evidence.result: Prospectively, runners who developed Achilles tendinopathy ran with less peak knee flexion and less peak DF.

compensations.text: Prolonged foot pronation (rearfoot eversion) through stance

evidence.citation: Becker J, James S, Wayner R, Osternig L, Chou LS 2017. Biomechanical Factors Associated With Achilles Tendinopathy and Medial Tibial Stress Syndrome in Runners. Am J Sports Med 45(11):2614-2621
evidence.result: Injured runners had both lower static DF ROM and longer eversion duration; association only, compensation not tested.

compensations.text: Early heel rise
compensations.note: No tested link found in running (clinical reasoning).

compensations.text: Shortened stride or forward trunk lean

screens.name: Weight-bearing lunge test (knee-to-wall)
screens.how: Foot facing the wall, heel down, lunge knee to touch wall; slide foot back to the furthest point the knee still touches with heel down; measure big toe-to-wall distance (cm) or tibia angle with an inclinometer; best of 3, both sides.
screens.positive_if: Use side-to-side difference and age/sex norms. A difference or change larger than measurement error (MDC about 1.6-1.9 cm or 4.6-4.7 deg; Powden 2015) is real. Age- and sex-specific percentile norms exist (McBride 2026, n=899: DF declines with age, males slightly higher, no left/right difference in healthy adults) but the numeric norms are in the full text, not the abstract. Popular cut-offs (e.g. <10 cm, >2 cm asymmetry) are NOT verified here.

evidence.citation: Bennell KL, Talbot RC, Wajswelner H, Techovanich W, Kelly DH, Hall AJ 1998. Intra-rater and inter-rater reliability of a weight-bearing lunge measure of ankle dorsiflexion. Aust J Physiother 44(3):175-180
evidence.result: Intra-rater ICC 0.97-0.98; inter-rater ICC 0.97 (angle) and 0.99 (distance).

evidence.citation: Powden CJ, Hoch JM, Hoch MC 2015. Reliability and minimal detectable change of the weight-bearing lunge test: A systematic review. Man Ther 20(4):524-32
evidence.result: Inter-clinician ICC 0.80-0.99, intra-clinician ICC 0.65-0.99; MDC 4.6 deg or 1.6 cm (inter) and 4.7 deg or 1.9 cm (intra).

evidence.citation: McBride S, Isabelle PL, Gomez-Carrion A, et al. 2026. International normative values for the weight-bearing lunge test across age and sex in 899 healthy adults. Musculoskelet Sci Pract 82:103525
evidence.result: Normative values by age and sex (n=899); no meaningful between-limb difference; performance declined with age, especially from 60-69 y; males slightly greater than females.

screens.name: Single-leg heel-raise test to fatigue (calf capacity)
screens.how: Stand on one leg on a 10-deg incline, fingertip support only, raise heel as high as possible at a set pace until fatigue; count reps each side.
screens.positive_if: Below age/sex norm: median 24 reps (men) and 21 (women) (Hebert-Losier 2017); median 25/24 (dominant/non-dominant) in Visser 2025. Between-day limits of agreement about +/-6 reps, so side differences smaller than ~6 reps may be noise.

evidence.citation: Hebert-Losier K, Wessman C, Alricsson M, Svantesson U 2017. Updated reliability and normative values for the standing heel-rise test in healthy adults. Physiotherapy 103(4):446-452
evidence.result: n=566; ICC 1.0; 95% LOA about -6.2 to 6.5 reps; median 24 (men) vs 21 (women); older women outperformed older men; younger, active men scored highest.

evidence.citation: Visser TSS, Neill SO, Hebert-Losier K, Eygendaal D, de Vos RJ 2025. Normative values for calf muscle strength-endurance in the general population assessed with the Calf Raise Application. Braz J Phys Ther 29(3):101188
evidence.result: n=500; median repetitions 25 (dominant) / 24 (non-dominant); no limb difference; lower with female sex, higher BMI, lower activity.

work.dose: e.g. 3 x 30 s each position, daily, 6 weeks
work.dose_source: 6-week duration from PMID 41169885 (healthy untrained men); hold time/sets: clinical practice, no trial (not stated in retrieved abstracts). Meta-analyses: PMID 16926259, 29223884
work.changes_running_pattern: not shown (PMID 26805699: an 8-week stretching programme did not alter running biomechanics in older runners vs control)

evidence.citation: Medeiros DM, Martini TF 2018. Chronic effect of different types of stretching on ankle dorsiflexion range of motion: Systematic review and meta-analysis. Foot (Edinb) 34:28-35
evidence.result: Chronic static stretching increased DF ROM by 5.17 deg (95% CI 4.39-5.95); PNF 4.32 deg; ballistic not significant.

evidence.citation: Radford JA, Burns J, Buchbinder R, Landorf KB, Cook C 2006. Does stretching increase ankle dorsiflexion range of motion? A systematic review. Br J Sports Med 40(10):870-5
evidence.result: Calf stretching gave small increases in DF: 2.07 deg (<=15 min total), 3.03 deg (15-30 min), 2.49 deg (>30 min); clinical importance unclear.

evidence.citation: Murakami Y, Konrad A, Kasahara K, et al. 2025. Comparison between 6 weeks of static stretching and resistance training programs on passive and active properties of plantar flexors. A randomized controlled trial. Front Physiol 16:1555253
evidence.result: 6 weeks static stretching increased DF ROM (d=0.65) and reduced passive stiffness; gains may be partly stretch tolerance.

work.item: Calf strengthening: heel raises / heavy-slow or eccentric heel drops, straight and bent knee
work.dose: e.g. 3 x 15 straight-knee + 3 x 15 bent-knee, progressed with load; 12 weeks for tendon cases (daily eccentric or 3 sessions/week heavy-slow)
work.dose_source: 12-week duration from PMID 9617396 and 26018970 (Achilles tendinopathy, not running mechanics); 6-week eccentric programme increased DF ROM in healthy people PMID 18091014; sets/reps not in retrieved abstracts: clinical practice, no trial
work.changes_running_pattern: not tested for DF/tibial progression; PMID 41980349 ankle-and-foot programme gave no clinically meaningful running kinematic change; PMID 31541409 no evidence strength gains transfer to running

evidence.citation: Mahieu NN, McNair P, Cools A, et al. 2008. Effect of eccentric training on the plantar flexor muscle-tendon tissue properties. Med Sci Sports Exerc 40(1):117-23
evidence.result: 6-week eccentric heel-drop programme increased DF ROM and reduced passive resistive torque; Achilles tendon stiffness unchanged.

evidence.citation: Murakami Y, Konrad A, Kasahara K, et al. 2025. Comparison between 6 weeks of static stretching and resistance training programs on passive and active properties of plantar flexors. A randomized controlled trial. Front Physiol 16:1555253
evidence.result: 6 weeks resistance training increased DF ROM (d=0.37) similar to stretching, plus strength and gastrocnemius thickness.

evidence.citation: Alfredson H, Pietila T, Jonsson P, Lorentzon R 1998. Heavy-load eccentric calf muscle training for the treatment of chronic Achilles tendinosis. Am J Sports Med 26(3):360-6
evidence.design: prospective case series with conventional-treatment comparison group (n=15+15)
evidence.result: 12 weeks heavy-load eccentric calf training: all 15 returned to full running, pain fell, calf strength symmetrical.

evidence.citation: Beyer R, Kongsgaard M, Hougs Kjaer B, et al. 2015. Heavy Slow Resistance Versus Eccentric Training as Treatment for Achilles Tendinopathy: A Randomized Controlled Trial. Am J Sports Med 43(7):1704-11
evidence.result: Heavy slow resistance and eccentric training (12 weeks) equally improved VISA-A and pain to 52 weeks; better compliance with HSR (92% vs 78%).

evidence.citation: Jarske H, Leppanen M, Avela J, et al. 2026. Effects of two pre-running training interventions on running kinematics and strength - A randomized controlled trial in novice recreational runners. Gait Posture 128:110174
evidence.result: 6-month hip-and-core or ankle-and-foot programmes vs static-stretching control: no between-group strength differences; kinematic changes <2 deg (hip IR); authors estimate 25-50% strength gain needed for a 2-deg kinematic change; not clinically meaningful.

work.item: Talocrural joint mobilisation (e.g. posterior glide / mobilisation with movement)
work.dose: e.g. 3-4 sets of 30-60 s or 10 reps, 1-2 sessions/week, 2-4 weeks
work.dose_source: clinical practice, no trial (retrieved meta-analysis PMID 30870009 is in chronic ankle instability and gives no dose in the abstract)
work.changes_running_pattern: not tested

evidence.citation: Vallandingham RA, Gaven SL, Powden CJ 2019. Changes in Dorsiflexion and Dynamic Postural Control After Mobilizations in Individuals With Chronic Ankle Instability: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. J Athl Train 54(4):403-417
evidence.design: systematic review + meta-analysis (10 studies, chronic ankle instability)
evidence.result: In chronic ankle instability, joint mobilisation improved DF ROM vs control with a weak-to-moderate effect (ES 0.41).

ankle_dorsiflexion.notes: Calf stretching and loading raise DF ROM by a few degrees, but no trial shows that this changes ankle or tibial angles during running. Treat a low running DF as a reason to screen (WBLT, heel-raise), not as proof of a restriction. Joachim 2024 is the best running-specific data (prospective) and links LOW DF and LOW knee flexion in running to later Achilles tendinopathy.

findings: reduced hip extension at late stance / toe-off

limitations.name: Hip flexor tightness (limited passive hip extension, Thomas test)

evidence.citation: Schache AG, Blanch PD, Murphy AT 2000. Relation of anterior pelvic tilt during running to clinical and kinematic measures of hip extension. Br J Sports Med 34(4):279-83
evidence.result: Thomas-test hip extension flexibility did NOT correlate with anterior pelvic tilt or with peak hip extension during running (elite athletes, 20 km/h).

evidence.citation: Mettler JH, Shapiro R, Pohl MB 2019. Effects of a Hip Flexor Stretching Program on Running Kinematics in Individuals With Limited Passive Hip Extension. J Strength Cond Res 33(12):3338-3344
evidence.result: 3-week home hip flexor stretching increased passive hip extension (p<0.001) but did NOT change running hip extension, anterior pelvic tilt or lumbar extension; change in passive ROM unrelated to running kinematics.

limitations.note: Tested and not supported: static hip flexor length does not predict or change running hip extension at submaximal speed. Possible role at near-maximal speed is untested (Mettler 2019).

limitations.name: Weak hip extensors (gluteus maximus)

evidence.citation: Teng HL, Powers CM 2016. Hip-Extensor Strength, Trunk Posture, and Use of the Knee-Extensor Muscles During Running. J Athl Train 51(7):519-24
evidence.result: OPPOSITE to the proposed chain: weaker hip extensors correlated with a MORE UPRIGHT trunk (r=0.55 with trunk flexion), less hip-extensor work and more knee-extensor work.

evidence.citation: Moffit TJ, Montgomery MM, Lockie RG, Pamukoff DN 2020. Association Between Knee- and Hip-Extensor Strength and Running-Related Injury Biomechanics in Collegiate Distance Runners. J Athl Train 55(12):1262-1269
evidence.result: Hip- and knee-extensor isometric strength not associated with forward trunk lean or hip kinematics in collegiate runners.

limitations.note: Tested; the data do not support 'weak glutes cause forward trunk lean'. If anything, stronger hip extensors go with more forward lean.

limitations.name: Trunk posture strategy (habit) - forward lean shifts work from knee to hip

evidence.citation: Teng HL, Powers CM 2014. Sagittal plane trunk posture influences patellofemoral joint stress during running. J Orthop Sports Phys Ther 44(10):785-92
evidence.result: Cueing more trunk flexion (14.1 deg) lowered peak patellofemoral joint stress; extended trunk (4.0 deg) raised it.

evidence.citation: Teng HL, Powers CM 2015. Influence of trunk posture on lower extremity energetics during running. Med Sci Sports Exerc 47(3):625-30
evidence.result: High trunk flexion runners (10.8 deg) had more hip-extensor energy generation and less knee-extensor energy absorption than low trunk flexion (3.6 deg).

evidence.citation: Bramah C, Preece SJ, Gill N, Herrington L 2018. Is There a Pathological Gait Associated With Common Soft Tissue Running Injuries? Am J Sports Med 46(12):3023-3031
evidence.result: Injured runners showed greater forward trunk lean at midstance than uninjured (association).

limitations.note: Trunk lean is a modifiable technique variable; more lean loads the hip/posterior chain and unloads the knee.

compensations.text: Anterior pelvic tilt coupled with reduced terminal-stance hip extension

evidence.citation: Schache AG, Blanch PD, Murphy AT 2000. Relation of anterior pelvic tilt during running to clinical and kinematic measures of hip extension. Br J Sports Med 34(4):279-83
evidence.result: Anterior pelvic tilt correlated with peak running hip extension (p<0.01): runners with less hip extension tended to show more anterior tilt.

compensations.text: Lumbar extension

evidence.citation: Mettler JH, Shapiro R, Pohl MB 2019. Effects of a Hip Flexor Stretching Program on Running Kinematics in Individuals With Limited Passive Hip Extension. J Strength Cond Res 33(12):3338-3344
evidence.result: Lumbar extension during running unchanged after hip flexor stretching.

compensations.text: Shortened stride / overstride

screens.name: Modified Thomas test (hip flexor length)
screens.how: Lie at the end of a plinth hugging one knee, keep the low back flat (pelvis neutral); let the other thigh hang; measure hip extension angle with a goniometer/inclinometer.
screens.positive_if: Thigh does not reach horizontal (hip extension below 0 deg) is the usual clinical criterion (not verified in retrieved abstracts). Healthy young adults averaged +5.4 deg (SD 9.7) with pelvis controlled (Eimiller 2024). A positive test does NOT predict running hip extension (Schache 2000).

evidence.citation: Eimiller K, Stoddard E, Janes B, Smith M, Vincek A 2024. Reliability of Goniometric Techniques for Measuring Hip Flexor Length Using the Modified Thomas Test. Int J Sports Phys Ther 19(8):997-1002
evidence.result: With pelvic tilt controlled: intra-rater ICC 0.911, inter-rater ICC 0.851; mean hip extension 5.43 +/- 9.73 deg (n=64).

evidence.citation: Gonzalez-de-la-Flor A, Seijas-Otero D 2026. Reliability of physical examination tests for assessing hip flexor flexibility: A systematic review and meta-analysis. PM R 18(7):779-792
evidence.result: Pooled intra-rater ICC 0.90, inter-rater 0.80 across hip flexor tests; high heterogeneity for Thomas/modified Thomas; Thomas test lowest inter-rater ICC 0.62.

screens.name: Prone hip extension strength (hand-held dynamometry)
screens.how: Prone, knee bent 90 deg, push the thigh up into a dynamometer (belt-fixed if possible), 3 maximal reps per side; normalise to body mass.
screens.positive_if: No verified normative cut-off. Use side-to-side difference beyond MDC (14-29% with belt fixation; Thorborg 2013).

evidence.citation: Thorborg K, Bandholm T, Holmich P 2013. Hip- and knee-strength assessments using a hand-held dynamometer with external belt-fixation are inter-tester reliable. Knee Surg Sports Traumatol Arthrosc 21(3):550-5
evidence.result: Belt-fixed HHD for hip abduction, adduction, flexion, extension: ICC 0.76-0.95; SEM 5-11%; MDC 14-29%.

evidence.citation: Ehresman BA, Lehecka BJ, Hiser D, Koster L, Wietharn J 2025. Improved Hip Flexibility and Gluteal Function Following a Daily Lunge-and-Reach Stretching Intervention. Int J Sports Phys Ther 20(6):814-823
evidence.design: cohort with randomised allocation to stretch or control (n=23), level 3
evidence.result: Prone hip extension HHD and modified Thomas test reliability ICC 0.92-0.99 in this study.

work.item: Trunk posture cue (adjust forward lean toward the target range; slight forward lean if knee-dominant pain)
work.dose: in-run cue during easy runs, e.g. 8 sessions over 2-3 weeks with feedback faded
work.dose_source: clinical practice, no trial (trunk-lean evidence is acute, single session)
work.changes_running_pattern: yes, acutely (PMID 25155651); no retraining trial for trunk lean

evidence.citation: Teng HL, Powers CM 2014. Sagittal plane trunk posture influences patellofemoral joint stress during running. J Orthop Sports Phys Ther 44(10):785-92
evidence.result: Runners could adopt flexed (14.1 deg) or extended (4.0 deg) trunk when cued; PFJ stress changed accordingly.

work.item: Glute max / hip extensor strengthening (e.g. bridges, hip thrust, step-ups, Romanian deadlift)
work.dose_source: 6-week hip-and-core protocol that increased hip extensor strength: PMID 25365133 (PFP); sets/reps not in abstract: clinical practice, no trial
work.changes_running_pattern: not tested for trunk lean or hip extension; cross-sectional data run opposite (PMID 27513169)

evidence.citation: Ferber R, Bolgla L, Earl-Boehm JE, Emery C, Hamstra-Wright K 2015. Strengthening of the hip and core versus knee muscles for the treatment of patellofemoral pain: a multicenter randomized controlled trial. J Athl Train 50(4):366-77
evidence.result: 6-week HIP protocol gained more hip abductor and extensor strength and earlier pain relief than KNEE protocol in PFP (n=199).

evidence.citation: Trowell D, Vicenzino B, Saunders N, Fox A, Bonacci J 2020. Effect of Strength Training on Biomechanical and Neuromuscular Variables in Distance Runners: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. Sports Med 50(1):133-150
evidence.result: Concurrent strength + endurance training increased knee flexor, plantarflexor, squat and knee extensor strength more than running alone; very limited evidence on stride parameters and no studies examined running biomechanics, so no evidence that strength adaptations transfer to running.

work.dose: 5 min daily, 6 weeks (Ehresman) or 3-week home programme (Mettler)
work.changes_running_pattern: no (PMID 29927892: passive hip extension improved, running hip extension and pelvic tilt unchanged)

evidence.citation: Ehresman BA, Lehecka BJ, Hiser D, Koster L, Wietharn J 2025. Improved Hip Flexibility and Gluteal Function Following a Daily Lunge-and-Reach Stretching Intervention. Int J Sports Phys Ther 20(6):814-823
evidence.design: cohort with randomised allocation to stretch or control (n=23), level 3
evidence.result: 5 min daily lunge-and-reach stretch for 6 weeks: modified Thomas test +5.9 deg; single-leg broad jump +12.4 cm; no change in glute strength or bridge endurance.

evidence.citation: Mettler JH, Shapiro R, Pohl MB 2019. Effects of a Hip Flexor Stretching Program on Running Kinematics in Individuals With Limited Passive Hip Extension. J Strength Cond Res 33(12):3338-3344
evidence.result: Stretching raised passive ROM without changing running kinematics.

hip_extension_trunk_lean.notes: Chain 12 (limited late-stance hip extension) is covered here because its evidence is the same: neither hip flexor length nor hip extensor strength has been shown to drive running hip extension or trunk lean; reduced running hip extension is coupled with anterior pelvic tilt (Schache 2000). The proposed chain 'hip flexor tightness/weak glute max -> forward lean' is contradicted rather than supported. Trunk lean is best treated as a technique variable (cue) with knee-vs-hip load trade-offs.

findings: high tibial inclination at initial contact
heel strike with large foot inclination

limitations.name: Low step rate (cadence) for the speed

evidence.citation: Anderson LM, Martin JF, Barton CJ, Bonanno DR 2022. What is the Effect of Changing Running Step Rate on Injury, Performance and Biomechanics? A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis. Sports Med Open 8(1):112
evidence.result: Increasing step rate: strong evidence of reduced peak knee flexion (SMD 0.66); moderate evidence of reduced step length (0.93), peak hip adduction (0.40), peak knee extensor moment (0.50) and foot strike angle (0.62); limited evidence of reduced braking impulse (0.64). Decreasing step rate: limited evidence of increased contact time (-0.95). Mostly immediate effects; injury/performance effects inconclusive.

evidence.citation: Heiderscheit BC, Chumanov ES, Michalski MP, Wille CM, Ryan MB 2011. Effects of step rate manipulation on joint mechanics during running. Med Sci Sports Exerc 43(2):296-302
evidence.result: Acute +5%/+10% step rate reduced step length, COM vertical excursion, braking impulse, peak knee flexion and knee energy absorption; at +10% peak hip adduction angle and hip adduction/IR moments also decreased.

limitations.note: Raising step rate shortens the step and reduces foot strike angle and braking; this is the only tested 'cause' of overstride. Evidence is mostly acute.

limitations.name: Limited hip control (hip flexor/glute function)
limitations.note: No tested link (clinical reasoning).

limitations.name: Limited trailing-side ankle dorsiflexion
limitations.note: No tested link.

compensations.text: Higher braking impulse and knee/hip energy absorption

evidence.citation: Heiderscheit BC, Chumanov ES, Michalski MP, Wille CM, Ryan MB 2011. Effects of step rate manipulation on joint mechanics during running. Med Sci Sports Exerc 43(2):296-302
evidence.result: Acute +5%/+10% step rate reduced step length, COM vertical excursion, braking impulse, peak knee flexion and knee energy absorption; at +10% peak hip adduction angle and hip adduction/IR moments also decreased.

screens.name: Step rate relative to speed
screens.how: Count steps per minute at the test speed and compare with speed- and sex-stratified reference values.
screens.positive_if: Below reference for the speed (Malisoux 2023 tables in full text; numbers not in abstract).

evidence.citation: Malisoux L, Napier C, Gette P, Delattre N, Theisen D 2023. Reference Values and Determinants of Spatiotemporal and Kinetic Variables in Recreational Runners. Orthop J Sports Med 11(10):23259671231204629
evidence.result: Speed- and sex-stratified reference values for cadence, contact time, vertical oscillation etc. in 860 recreational runners; running speed was the only strong determinant (r>0.7).

work.dose: +10% step rate, metronome, on all runs; reassess at 4 weeks

evidence.citation: Anderson LM, Martin JF, Barton CJ, Bonanno DR 2022. What is the Effect of Changing Running Step Rate on Injury, Performance and Biomechanics? A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis. Sports Med Open 8(1):112
evidence.result: Increasing step rate: strong evidence of reduced peak knee flexion (SMD 0.66); moderate evidence of reduced step length (0.93), peak hip adduction (0.40), peak knee extensor moment (0.50) and foot strike angle (0.62); limited evidence of reduced braking impulse (0.64). Decreasing step rate: limited evidence of increased contact time (-0.95). Mostly immediate effects; injury/performance effects inconclusive.

evidence.citation: Bramah C, Preece SJ, Gill N, Herrington L 2019. A 10% Increase in Step Rate Improves Running Kinematics and Clinical Outcomes in Runners With Patellofemoral Pain at 4 Weeks and 3 Months. Am J Sports Med 47(14):3406-3413
evidence.result: Single session, +10% step rate with metronome, self-monitored with GPS watch: at follow-up pelvic drop -3.1 deg, hip adduction -4.0 deg, knee flexion -4.1 deg; pain and function improved, maintained at 3 months. Case series, no control.

evidence.citation: Doyle E, Doyle TLA, Bonacci J, Fuller JT 2022. The Effectiveness of Gait Retraining on Running Kinematics, Kinetics, Performance, Pain, and Injury in Distance Runners: A Systematic Review With Meta-analysis. J Orthop Sports Phys Ther 52(4):192-206
evidence.result: Moderate certainty: step-rate retraining increased step rate (SMD 1.03) and reduced average vertical loading rate (SMD -0.57). Two trials showed reduced 1-year injury incidence.

work.changes_running_pattern: not tested

evidence.citation: Trowell D, Vicenzino B, Saunders N, Fox A, Bonacci J 2020. Effect of Strength Training on Biomechanical and Neuromuscular Variables in Distance Runners: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. Sports Med 50(1):133-150
evidence.result: Concurrent strength + endurance training increased knee flexor, plantarflexor, squat and knee extensor strength more than running alone; very limited evidence on stride parameters and no studies examined running biomechanics, so no evidence that strength adaptations transfer to running.

work.changes_running_pattern: not tested

overstride.notes: Moderate evidence only for step rate as the modifiable driver. Hip control and trailing-side dorsiflexion as causes of overstride: no tested link.

findings: high knee frontal-plane projection angle (2D valgus)

limitations.name: Weak hip abductors / external rotators

evidence.result: 19 studies (17 cross-sectional, 2 interventions with notable limitations): insufficient support for a consistent association between hip abductor/ER strength and running biomechanics in healthy runners, and no convincing evidence that strengthening these muscles alone changes running kinematics or kinetics.
